title: When you miss a day
hookLine: the tradition expects stumbling; you simply begin again
tomorrow: a sage warned a fixed prayer can go dead. so do you change it?

lines: MISS ONE MORNING: BACK TO ZERO.
cards: Streak counters are ruthless. Miss one morning and the number you were proud of drops back to zero, and quitting starts to look reasonable. The Torah has a much bigger miss.
Moses comes down the mountain, sees the golden calf, and smashes the first tablets. Later he carves a new pair, and God writes the same words again. So far, a clean restart.
But the Talmud adds a strange detail: the broken pieces were kept too. Why keep the broken pieces?

teach.h: WHOLE AND BROKEN, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Both went into the Ark, the Talmud says: the whole tablets and the broken ones, side by side, in the Ark itself. And it draws its own lesson from that, about people.
Honor an elder who has forgotten his learning through no fault of his own, because the broken tablets also rest in the Ark. Brokenness doesn't get thrown out. It gets carried, with honor.
Proverbs puts the same idea in one line: a righteous person falls seven times, and rises up again. Read it slowly. Falling is inside the sentence.
Seven times, even. The verse doesn't define the righteous as the ones who never fall; it defines them as the ones who get up.
So when you miss a day, the tradition isn't surprised, and it doesn't send you back to zero.

The missed days go into the box with the good ones, and you begin again from where you are, not from the start. Something to tell a friend tonight: in the Ark, the broken tablets sat right next to the whole ones.

how: Jewish teaching on teshuvah, returning, expects lapses: someone who misses prayers, study or a practice is taught to pick it up again at the next opportunity rather than abandon it; Elul and the High Holy Days give the whole community a set time to begin again.

games.q: what does “when you miss a day” mean?
o: picking a practice back up after a lapse
taking a planned rest day from a routine
making up every missed day before going on

games.q: broken and kept — tap the pairs.
p: held whole tablets and broken ones
honor an elder who forgot his learning

s: in Jewish practice, a missed day means starting over from zero
the broken tablets stayed in the Ark beside the whole ones; nothing went back to zero.
Proverbs pictures a righteous person falling seven times
and rising up again; the rising is what makes them righteous.
the Talmud says the broken tablets were buried outside the camp
it says they were kept in the Ark, beside the new ones.

games.q: your dad stopped his daily walk three weeks ago after a bad cold, and now he says he's 'just not a walker.' what does Proverbs 24:16 point him toward?
o: he's probably right; three weeks shows it wasn't really his thing.
walk tomorrow; falling is part of the sentence, and so is rising.
make up all the missed walks before calling himself a walker again.
games.why: the verse defines the righteous by getting up, not by never falling. no reset, no make-up debt: begin again.

practice: If you're able, sit all the way down, and let yourself settle as if you'd just stumbled. Then stand slowly, feeling your feet take your weight again.
Sit, and rise, once or twice more, without hurrying: the falling is in the sentence, and so is the rising.

wordCard.voice: When you miss a day: the tradition expects it. The broken days are kept, not erased, and you begin again from where you stand.

orig.note: Hebrew, Proverbs 24:16: for a righteous one falls seven times, and rises.

carryVoice: For the road: begin again. The broken days ride along in the Ark; they don't send you back to zero.

sources.ref: Exodus 32:19 and 34:1 (the first tablets broken; the second pair carved, with the same words)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8b (honor an elder who forgot his learning; the tablets and the broken tablets were placed in the Ark)
Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b (the tablets and the broken tablets in the Ark)
Proverbs 24:16 (a righteous person falls seven times and rises)
